text:
The A B test is live, its users split at random between the old checkout and a new one, and the readout says the new one won. Someone wants to ship it today. Look closer first. The two groups aren't the size you asked for. It's only week one. And this was the best of ten metrics. Any one of those can turn a win into nothing. This round is about experiments once they're running: fourteen questions. Ten get a figure each. The other four are short enough to take in passing.

Question one. What are the common A B testing pitfalls? Five come up again and again: a split that isn't the one you set, segments that disagree with the total, a lift that fades once it isn't new, metrics read until one of them moves, and users who affect each other. Each gets a question of its own here.

Question two. What is a sample ratio mismatch, and what causes it? You asked for fifty-fifty, and got four thousand eight hundred against five thousand two hundred. A chi-square test asks whether chance could do that. Here chi-square is sixteen, and p is about one in sixteen thousand. That's a sample ratio mismatch, an S R M. Four thousand nine hundred sixty against five thousand forty would be chance: p is point four two. A mismatch means something treats the arms differently: bots filtered from one arm, a redirect that loses slow page loads, a logging bug. Find it before you read a single result.
